# Population, Sample, Census and Sampling Frame {#sec-population-sample-frame}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Define target and accessible populations.
- Identify problems caused by incomplete sampling frames.
:::

## The idea

The **target population** is the population to which results are intended to apply. The **accessible population** is reached through the actual recruitment setting. The **sampling frame** is the list or operational mechanism from which sampling occurs. A **census** attempts to observe all eligible members of a defined population; a sample observes a subset.

## When and how to apply it

The intended inference must match the selection mechanism. A hospital-based consecutive sample is not a random sample of every person with the disease in the district. Even perfect arithmetic for sample size cannot repair a mismatch between target population and sampling frame.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
Consider hypertension prevalence among all district adults, among patients registered at one health centre, and among patients visiting that centre on study days. Each is a different target.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
A known hospital footfall is not automatically the finite population size appropriate for a finite population correction.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Draw a three-level diagram: target population → accessible population → analysed sample. Annotate inclusion, exclusion and non-participation.

## Key message

The sampling frame determines who can be sampled; it does not by itself establish generalisability.
